title: HCI Module 7 — Past & Future of HCI, Perceptual Interfaces, Context-Awareness
description: Exam revision: past, present and future of HCI, Moore's law vs UIs, evolution of interfaces, perceptual user interfaces, context-awareness and perception.
endCard: 📘 Past, present & future of HCI — revised. You've got this!

scenes.title: Intro

viz.s: From a 1000 kg computer to rooms that understand you

lines: Computers once weighed a thousand kilograms. Soon, whole rooms will understand you. How did we get here?
This module covers the past, present and future of HCI,
then perceptual interfaces, context awareness, and perception.

scenes.title: 1. The past

items.b:
by Konrad Zuse — improved version of Z1 & Z2
• statistical analysis of wing flutter
• weighed ≈ 1000 kg
• memory: 64 words of 22 bits

first fully electronic, general-purpose computer
• filled 1000 sq ft of floor
• 5000 additions/subtractions per second
• artillery firing tables, US Army Ballistic Research Lab

lines: The past. Back in nineteen forty-one, the earliest computer was the Zuse Z3, invented by Konrad Zuse.
It improved on the Z1 and Z2, and was used for statistical analysis of wing flutter.
It weighed around one thousand kilograms, and its memory held just sixty-four words of twenty-two bits.
Then ENIAC, announced in nineteen forty-six, the first fully electronic, general purpose computer.
It filled one thousand square feet, and could do five thousand simple additions and subtractions per second.
It was mainly used to calculate artillery firing tables for the US Army Ballistic Research Laboratory.

scenes.title: 2. The present — user-centred

events.b: LED display · 8 h standby · shows only numbers · recalls 30 numbers

lines: The present. HCI inventions today are user centred, from entertainment to communication, built for a richer user experience.
Video game consoles exist purely for entertainment. It started with the nineteen seventy-two Magnavox Odyssey, followed by the famous Atari,
and today, highly interactive consoles like the PlayStation four.
Mobile phones are another HCI device. The first was the Motorola DynaTAC: an LED display, eight hours of standby, showing only numbers to dial, and recalling only thirty phone numbers.

scenes.title: 3. The future

nodes.b: more integrated interaction — never miss anything important

lines: The future. Interaction will be interactive and integrated, so we don't miss anything important.
From workspaces to the living home, human interaction with computers will be more integrated, with full involvement.
All this will make life easier, with better productivity, as in Microsoft's Productivity Future Vision video from twenty eleven.

scenes.title: 4. Perceptual interfaces — no Moore's Law for UIs
lines: Why perceptual interfaces? Moore's law has driven computer hardware for decades, with exponential improvement.
Five years gives about ten times improvement, ten years a hundred times, and twenty years ten thousand times.
But there has been no Moore's law for user interfaces. They have barely changed.

scenes.title: 5. Evolution of user interfaces
lines: The evolution of user interfaces. In the nineteen fifties: switches and punched cards, with no paradigm at all.
In the nineteen seventies: the command line interface, with the typewriter as its paradigm.
In the nineteen eighties: the graphical user interface, with the desktop paradigm.
And the two thousands? The slide leaves question marks. The answer this module points to is perceptual interfaces, using natural human abilities.

scenes.title: 6. Current UI limitations

items.b: today's UIs use a fraction of how we sense, speak, gesture and express
emails, videoconferencing, videophones, computer conferencing, chat rooms, IM
text-based — users communicate exclusively using text
do conversational rules apply in tech-mediated talk?
how do people repair them — phone, email, IM, text?

lines: The main limitation of current interfaces is a failure to use human abilities.
Even when communicating across locations, we rely on emails, video conferencing, videophones, computer conferencing, chat rooms and instant messaging.
MUDs and MOOs were text based, so users communicated exclusively using text.
So ask: in technology mediated conversations, do the same rules apply, are there more breakdowns, and how do people repair them?

scenes.title: 7. New paradigms (context & perception)

items.b: wearable computers, Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality
coupling physical objects with digital data
computers that understand and express emotion

viz.note: I U T M A — “I Use Touch, Mic, Affect”

lines: Five emerging paradigms. Immersive environments: wearable computers, virtual reality, augmented reality.
Ubiquitous computing: invisible and pervasive.
Tangible user interfaces: coupling physical objects with digital data.
Multimodal interfaces: sound, speech, gesture.
And affective computing: computers that understand and express emotion.

scenes.title: 8. Context-awareness

nodes.b: context-awareness is a key characteristic of perceptual interfaces
interaction is improvised and dynamic, not scripted
interactions among applications are based on the specific context

lines: Context awareness is a key characteristic of perceptual interfaces.
Interaction becomes improvised and dynamic,
and interactions among applications are based on the specific context.

scenes.title: 9. Perception — the 5 W's

viz.note: Interfaces must adapt to the overall situation AND the individual user

lines: Perception. To respond appropriately, objects and rooms need to pay attention to people,
and to context.
Machines must be aware of their environment: who, what, when, where, and why.
And interfaces must be adaptive, to the overall situation, and to the individual user.

scenes.title: 10. Media spaces

items.b: audio + video + computer systems that “extend the world of desks, chairs, walls and ceilings”

lines: Media spaces, under dialog semantics and design, combine audio, video and computer systems to extend the world of desks, chairs, walls and ceilings.
Examples are Xerox Media Space, Hydra, Cruiser, and the VideoWindow system.

scenes.title: 11. Perceptual User Interfaces (PUI)
lines: Perceptual user interfaces were featured in a special section of Communications of the ACM, March two thousand, edited by Matthew Turk and George Robertson.
PUIs combine natural human capabilities, communication, motor, cognitive and perceptual skills, with computer input and output, machine perception, and reasoning.
They integrate research from vision, speech, graphics and visualisation, user modelling, haptics and cognitive psychology. Maybe one day, taste and smell.

scenes.title: Recap

viz.s: Past → Present → Future → Perceptual, context-aware interfaces

lines: Quick recap.
From the Z3 and ENIAC, to consoles and the DynaTAC, hardware grew exponentially while interfaces stalled, from punched cards to command line to GUI.
The future is perceptual, context aware interfaces that know who, what, when, where and why. You've got this.
